decision.explanation: Factor y=x(3-x)(x+2), giving zeros at -2, 0, and 3. The curve is below the x-axis on (-2,0) and above it on (0,3), so total area requires negating the first integral and adding the second.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14038781/assets/c1906d5ad1ab55a028bcdb163e3066788dea44d928a53fda493ffe8972d369b6.png)

Which integral expression gives the total area enclosed between the curve $y=6x+{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above?
after.worked_solution:
First, we the limits of integration. We find the $x$-intercepts of the curve as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}6x+{x}^{2}-{x}^{3} & =0 \\ -x({x}^{2}-x-6) & =0 \\ x(x+2)(x-3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $x=-2$, $x=0$ or $x=3.$ 
This gives us two regions:

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=0.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=3.$

Notice that for $x\in [-2,0]$ the region lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-2}^{0}(6x+{x}^{2}-{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
{A}_{1}=-{\int }_{-2}^{0}(6x+{x}^{2}-{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-2}^{0}-(6x+{x}^{2}-{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x.
$$

For $x\in [0,3]$, we have

$$
{A}_{2}={\int }_{0}^{3}(6x+{x}^{2}-{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x.
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}={\int }_{-2}^{0}-(6x+{x}^{2}-{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{3}(6x+{x}^{2}-{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x.
$$

Question 1

Which integral expression gives the total area enclosed between the curve y=6x+x2−x3 and the x-axis, as shown above?

a
∫−10−(6x+x2−x3)dx+∫02(6x+x2−x3)dx
b
∫−10(6x+x2−x3)dx+∫02−(6x+x2−x3)dx
c
∫−20−(6x+x2−x3)dx+∫03(6x+x2−x3)dx
d
∫−20(6x+x2−x3)dx+∫03−(6x+x2−x3)dx
e
∫−23(6x+x2−x3)dx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we the limits of integration. We find the x-intercepts of the curve as follows:

6x+x2−x3=0−x(x2−x−6)=0x(x+2)(x−3)=0.

So we have x=−2, x=0 or x=3. This gives us two regions:

  • The area between the curve and the x-axis from x=−2 to x=0.

  • The area between the curve and the x-axis from x=0 to x=3.

Notice that for x∈[−2,0] the region lies completely below the x-axis. Hence, the value of ∫aby(x)dx=∫−20(6x+x2−x3)dx will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by A1=−∫−20(6x+x2−x3)dx=∫−20−(6x+x2−x3)dx.

For x∈[0,3], we have A2=∫03(6x+x2−x3)dx.

Finally, the total area is A=A1+A2=∫−20−(6x+x2−x3)dx+∫03(6x+x2−x3)dx.

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14038781/assets/c1906d5ad1ab55a028bcdb163e3066788dea44d928a53fda493ffe8972d369b6.png)

Which integral expression gives the total area enclosed between the curve $y=6x+{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}$ and the $x$-axis, as shown above?
content.worked_solution:
First, we the limits of integration. We find the $x$-intercepts of the curve as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}6x+{x}^{2}-{x}^{3} & =0 \\ -x({x}^{2}-x-6) & =0 \\ x(x+2)(x-3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $x=-2$, $x=0$ or $x=3.$ 
This gives us two regions:

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=0.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=0$ to $x=3.$

Notice that for $x\in [-2,0]$ the region lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-2}^{0}(6x+{x}^{2}-{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
{A}_{1}=-{\int }_{-2}^{0}(6x+{x}^{2}-{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-2}^{0}-(6x+{x}^{2}-{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x.
$$

For $x\in [0,3]$, we have

$$
{A}_{2}={\int }_{0}^{3}(6x+{x}^{2}-{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x.
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}={\int }_{-2}^{0}-(6x+{x}^{2}-{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{3}(6x+{x}^{2}-{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x.
$$

after.problem: Find the total area of the region between the curve $y={x}^{3}-1$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=3.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-1 & =0 \\ {x}^{3} & =1 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Since $1\in [-1,3]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=1.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=1$ to $x=3.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14038781/assets/0d7fcf48509464cdd6c22962b11c3db4fe24a08fa285adeeb9e30114c9667f49.png)

Notice that the region for $x\in [-1,1]$ lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{3}-1)\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =-{\int }_{-1}^{1}({x}^{3}-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-x)|}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =-([\frac{1}{4}-1]-[\frac{1}{4}+1]) \\  & =-(-\frac{3}{4}-\frac{5}{4}) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\in [1,3],$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}({x}^{3}-1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}-x)|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =[\frac{81}{4}-3]-[\frac{1}{4}-1] \\  & =\frac{69}{4}+\frac{3}{4} \\  & =18.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=2+18=20.
$$

after.problem: Find the total area of the region between the curve $y={x}^{5}+{x}^{2}$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=0.$
after.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{5}+{x}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}({x}^{3}+1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=0$ and $x=-1$ are our real solutions. Since $-1\in [-2,0]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=-1.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=0.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14038781/assets/dc57ac72bdc0d496dc9e106c87d9c5f60cd5d8ca11d150f061edda690082cc71.png)

Notice that for $x\in [-2,-1]$ the region lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-2}^{-1}({x}^{5}+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =-{\int }_{-2}^{-1}({x}^{5}+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{-2}^{-1}{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{-2}^{-1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{x}^{6}}{6}{|}_{-2}^{-1}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}{|}_{-2}^{-1} \\  & =-[\frac{(-1)^{6}}{6}-\frac{(-2)^{6}}{6}]-[\frac{(-1)^{3}}{3}-\frac{(-2)^{3}}{3}] \\  & =\frac{21}{2}-\frac{7}{3} \\  & =\frac{49}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\in [-1,0]$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}({x}^{5}+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{-1}^{0}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{6}}{6}{|}_{-1}^{0}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}{|}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =[0-\frac{(-1)^{6}}{6}]+[0-\frac{(-1)^{3}}{3}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=\frac{49}{6}+\frac{1}{6}=\frac{25}{3}.
$$

content.problem: Find the total area of the region between the curve $y={x}^{5}+{x}^{2}$ and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=0.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we find the intersections of the curve with the $x$-axis:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{5}+{x}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}({x}^{3}+1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=0$ and $x=-1$ are our real solutions. Since $-1\in [-2,0]$, we have two regions: 

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-2$ to $x=-1.$

- The area between the curve and the $x$-axis from $x=-1$ to $x=0.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14038781/assets/dc57ac72bdc0d496dc9e106c87d9c5f60cd5d8ca11d150f061edda690082cc71.png)

Notice that for $x\in [-2,-1]$ the region lies completely below the $x$-axis. Hence, the value of

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-2}^{-1}({x}^{5}+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x
$$

will be negative. Therefore, the area that we want is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{1} & =-{\int }_{-2}^{-1}({x}^{5}+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{-2}^{-1}{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{-2}^{-1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{{x}^{6}}{6}{|}_{-2}^{-1}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}{|}_{-2}^{-1} \\  & =-[\frac{(-1)^{6}}{6}-\frac{(-2)^{6}}{6}]-[\frac{(-1)^{3}}{3}-\frac{(-2)^{3}}{3}] \\  & =\frac{21}{2}-\frac{7}{3} \\  & =\frac{49}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\in [-1,0]$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{2} & ={\int }_{a}^{b}y(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}({x}^{5}+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{-1}^{0}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{6}}{6}{|}_{-1}^{0}+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}{|}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =[0-\frac{(-1)^{6}}{6}]+[0-\frac{(-1)^{3}}{3}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the total area is

$$
A={A}_{1}+{A}_{2}=\frac{49}{6}+\frac{1}{6}=\frac{25}{3}.
$$
